passages.t: A great light, and a child born to reign
passages.happening:
After the darkness of chapter 8: ‘Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress’ (verse 1). God humbled the land of Zebulun and Naphtali in the past, but he will honor ‘the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations’ (verse 1).

‘The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned’ (verse 2). God has multiplied the nation and its joy, like joy at harvest (verse 3). ‘For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden’ (verse 4). Every soldier's boot and every garment rolled in blood will be burned (verse 5).

‘For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace’ (verse 6). ‘Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end’ (verse 7). He will reign on David's throne with justice and righteousness forever. ‘The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Zebulun and Naphtali were tribal lands in Galilee, west and southwest of the Sea of Galilee. They were the first parts of Israel to fall to Assyria. In 733 and 732 BC Tiglath-pileser III annexed the north and organized it into provinces named for their capitals: Dor on the coast, the Way of the Sea; Megiddo, governing Galilee; and Gilead, beyond the Jordan. The three names in verse 1 match those districts closely. The first land to go dark is promised the first light.

The day of Midian recalls Gideon's victory, when God cut his army down to three hundred so that Israel could not boast that its own hand had saved it. The yoke and the rod come from the language of forced labor, the same words used of the taskmasters of Egypt.

In the ancient world a king's accession came with throne names. Egyptian pharaohs received a set of formal names at coronation, and Judah spoke of its king as God's son on the day he was crowned. Some scholars think the four names of verse 6 reflect such a practice. Even so, the titles go beyond anything claimed for a king of Judah. Mighty God is used of the LORD himself in the next chapter.

Ahaz had hired an empire to carry his government for him. This child carries it on his own shoulders. The yoke on the people's shoulder in verse 4 is replaced by the government on the child's shoulder in verse 6.
passages.later: Matthew sees verses 1 and 2 fulfilled when Jesus made his home in Galilee: ‘the people living in darkness have seen a great light’ (Matthew 4:16). The angel tells Mary that God ‘will give Him the throne of His father David’ and that ‘His kingdom will never end’ (Luke 1:32-33). And Isaiah uses the title of verse 6 for God himself in the next chapter, where a remnant will return ‘to the Mighty God’ (Isaiah 10:21).
passages.hard:
Were the titles of verse 6 meant for a human king of Isaiah's day, or for a divine Messiah?

The case for a human king is historical and grammatical. The poem uses the language of royal birth and accession, and scholars such as Gerhard von Rad and Albrecht Alt read it as an accession oracle for a king of Judah. Jewish tradition from the Talmud to Rashi and Ibn Ezra identified the child with Hezekiah, the faithful son of faithless Ahaz, whose deliverance in 701 BC answered the darkness of the Assyrian crisis. The Targum and Rashi divide the words so that Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God and Everlasting Father describe God, who names the child Prince of Peace, and modern Jewish translations render the whole as a sentence about God. Some critical scholars who give all the titles to the child take Mighty God as godlike hero, and note that royal language in the ancient world was often extravagant.

Christian interpreters answer that the same phrase, El Gibbor, is used of the LORD himself in 10:21, and of God in Deuteronomy and Jeremiah. The reign described has no end and its peace no limit, which no king of Judah fulfilled; Hezekiah's own reign ended with the prophecy of exile. Commentators such as John Oswalt and J. Alec Motyer conclude that the child is the divine Messiah. Others take a middle path: the oracle may have been spoken for the royal hope of Isaiah's day, but its language deliberately outruns any son of David then living, so that the hope remained open until the New Testament found it realized in Jesus.

These notes set out each reading in its holders' terms. The church confesses Jesus as Son of David and as God, a confession that rests on the whole New Testament and not on this verse alone.
passages.asks: The child in this chapter carries the government on his own shoulders. Ask what you are carrying that you were never meant to carry. And ask which of his four names you most need him to be for you now.

passages.t: Bricks fallen, and Israel's proud answer
passages.happening:
The tone changes. ‘The Lord has sent a message against Jacob, and it has fallen upon Israel’ (verse 8). The people of Ephraim and Samaria will know it, though they answer with pride (verse 9): ‘The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone; the sycamores have been felled, but we will replace them with cedars’ (verse 10).

So the LORD raises up Rezin's enemies against him (verse 11). ‘Aram from the east and Philistia from the west have devoured Israel with open mouths. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The second half of the chapter returns to the present and begins a poem against Israel, the northern kingdom, in its last years before the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. Its refrain, that God's anger is not turned away and his hand is still raised, first appeared in 5:25 and runs on into chapter 10.

Israel's answer to its first losses was defiant confidence. Mud bricks and sycamore beams were the ordinary building materials. Cut stone and cedar were the materials of palaces. The people say they will rebuild bigger and better. The first hearers would have recognized the boast: they had heard it in their own streets.

The poem is a warning about a people that will not learn from what is happening to it.
passages.later: Amos, prophesying in the north a little earlier, saw the same pattern: God sent famine, drought and plague, ‘yet you did not return to Me,’ declares the LORD (Amos 4:6).
passages.asks: Israel answered loss with a boast that it would rebuild bigger. Ask how you have answered your own losses. And ask whether you have ever tried to build your way out of something God was using to call you back.

passages.t: Leaders who mislead, and a people devouring itself
passages.happening:
‘But the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 13). So the LORD will cut off head and tail, palm branch and reed, in a single day (verse 14). ‘The head is the elder and honorable man, and the tail is the prophet who teaches lies’ (verse 15). ‘For those who guide this people mislead them, and those they mislead are swallowed up’ (verse 16). The refrain sounds again (verse 17).

Wickedness burns like a fire through thorns and forest (verse 18). The land is scorched, and no one spares his brother (verse 19). They grab on the right and on the left and are never satisfied, each one turning on his own (verse 20). ‘Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they turn against Judah. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The northern kingdom's politics were violent. Four of its last six kings were assassinated: Zechariah by Shallum, Shallum by Menahem, Menahem's son by Pekah, and Pekah by Hoshea. Manasseh and Ephraim, the two great northern tribes, were brothers by descent, sons of Joseph. Picturing them devouring each other was a fair description of those coups.

The head and the tail are named. The leaders and the false prophets who should have guided the people misled them, and those who followed were swallowed up.

Verse 17 says the Lord has no pity even on the fatherless and widows, the very people he elsewhere defends. In its setting it is a measure of how far the whole society had gone. It is not a statement that God is indifferent to the vulnerable, which the rest of the book denies again and again.

Verse 20 uses the picture of people consuming their own to describe a society turning on itself in hunger and civil war. These notes do not linger on it.
passages.later: Kings records the bloodshed of these years, ending when ‘Hoshea attacked Pekah, killed him, and reigned in his place’ (2 Kings 15:30). And Isaiah's poem goes on into the next chapter with the same refrain (Isaiah 10:4).
passages.asks: The people did not return to the one who struck them. Ask whether hardship has driven you toward God or away. And ask whose guidance you follow, and whether it leads you to God or swallows you up.
